Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Support individuals or groups in accessing essential services and resources
Situation2: They encounter a situation where someone urgently needs housing, medical help, or protection and must be connected to services quickly.
Story: My phone buzzed at 2 a.m., jolting me awake. It was Maya, her voice trembling as she told me her father had just been rushed to the hospital. She needed me to listen, to be there, to help her hold the pieces together. I sat up, heart pounding, trying to offer comfort, asking gentle questions, letting her cry. Then, as I tried to focus on her words, another call came through—an emergency from the shelter. A young woman with a child had just arrived, fleeing an abusive home, desperate for a safe place and medical attention. As an advocate, I was the on-call contact, expected to coordinate immediate help. My mind raced. Maya’s sobs filled my ear, but the shelter’s message blinked insistently. I felt torn in two, the weight of both needs pressing down on me. I wanted to be the friend Maya needed, but I also knew the woman at the shelter was depending on me. My hands shook as I stared at my phone, caught between two urgent calls for help, unsure which role to answer first.
